title: Crime and Society
in30Seconds: Crime is behavior that violates official law and is punishable through formal sanctions — the working definition used in OpenStax's Introduction to Sociology. Crime is not the same as deviance: deviance breaks social norms, while crime breaks written law. Sociologists sort crime into violent, property, white-collar, and debated victimless types, and they count it two ways — through police reports (the FBI's UCR) and through surveys (the BJS's NCVS). Rates vary by place, age, and circumstance, and fear of crime can outrun the data.
whyItMatters: Academically, crime sits at the intersection of core sociological ideas: norms and law, social control, and the question of how societies define and measure behavior. Practically, crime statistics shape how people vote, where they live, what they fear, and how they judge their neighbors — so knowing what the numbers can and cannot say matters for everyday citizenship. And it matters forward-looking: as societies debate public safety, the quality of the conversation depends on understanding that crime data are a mirror held up by institutions and by the people who decide what to report. Learning to read that mirror is a skill for any course, any career, and any news cycle.
learningObjectives: Define crime using the working definition: behavior that violates official law and is punishable through formal sanctions.
Distinguish crime from deviance, using an original example of behavior that is one but not the other.
Identify violent, property, white-collar, and debated victimless crimes, each with an original example.
Explain how the UCR and the NCVS count crime differently, and why neither captures all crime.
Analyze the gap between public fear of crime and official crime data, using attributed survey findings.

collegeVersion.heading: What crime is
collegeVersion.body: Sociologists use a working definition: crime is behavior that violates official law and is punishable through formal sanctions (OpenStax, Introduction to Sociology 3e, section 7.3). Three details matter. First, the law is official: societies maintain legal codes — rules adopted and enforced by a political authority — and breaking them carries formal consequences such as fines or imprisonment. Second, the definition is behavioral: it describes what people do. Third, it is social: what counts as a crime is decided by a society at a particular time and place. Original example: a cyclist who rolls through a stop sign on an empty street at dawn has broken official law and is formally punishable.

collegeVersion.heading: Crime and deviance: illegal versus norm-violating
collegeVersion.body: Deviance and crime are siblings, not synonyms. Deviance is a violation of social norms — the shared expectations about how people should behave; crime is a violation of formal law (OpenStax 7.3). The two circles overlap: most crimes also violate norms, and many norm violations break no law. OpenStax offers a clean pairing: walking to class backward is deviant — people stare — yet it is not a crime; driving with a blood-alcohol level above the state's limit is a crime. Original example: a student who wears sandals to a job interview commits no crime, though interviewers may read it as poor judgment; the same student who signs the interviewer's name to a form commits a crime, however harmless the intent. The deeper study of deviance belongs to its own topic. Here the boundary is enough: illegal versus norm-violating.

collegeVersion.heading: The types of crime
collegeVersion.body: Sociologists sort crime into broad categories. Violent crimes are based on the use of force or the threat of force — murder, rape, armed robbery (OpenStax 7.3). Original example: holding up a convenience-store clerk with a knife is a violent crime — the threat of force is present. Nonviolent, or property, crimes involve the destruction or theft of property without force — larceny, car theft, vandalism. Original example: slashing a parked car's tires is a property crime; no force was aimed at a person. White-collar, or corporate, crime is committed by people working in a business environment — embezzlement, insider trading, identity theft (OpenStax 7.3). Original example: a payroll clerk who reroutes a few cents from every employee paycheck into her own account is embezzling. Victimless crime is a debated category: illegal acts in which the person committing them is not explicitly harming anyone else — underage drinking, selling a sexual act — and critics argue such acts do harm society (OpenStax 7.3). Original example: an 18-year-old drinks a beer where the legal age is 21; there is no victim in the room, but the law is broken. Whether the label fits is an open public debate, not a settled fact.

collegeVersion.heading: Who is counted: police reports and surveys
collegeVersion.body: The United States has no single count of crime; its two main national measures work differently (Pew Research Center). The Uniform Crime Reports (UCR), published by the FBI, compile crimes reported to law enforcement: the FBI gathers data from thousands of police agencies nationwide and publishes annual totals (OpenStax 7.3). The honest limit: the UCR only sees what people report. Many crimes go unreported — out of fear, shame, distrust of police, or the belief that nothing would be done. The National Crime Victimization Survey (NCVS), run by the Bureau of Justice Statistics, takes the other route: each year it interviews a nationally representative sample of about 240,000 people in about 150,000 households, age 12 and older (BJS). Because it asks people directly, the NCVS captures crimes never reported to police — and shows more crime than police reports do. Its limits: it cannot count murder, and it misses people without stable addresses. Neither measure is complete; each is a partial picture from a different angle.

collegeVersion.heading: The social patterns
collegeVersion.body: Crime is not spread evenly; it varies by place, age, and circumstance. Place: in 2022, FBI data showed more than 700 violent crimes per 100,000 residents in New Mexico and Alaska, versus fewer than 200 per 100,000 in Rhode Island, Connecticut, New Hampshire, and Maine; the FBI notes local factors such as population density and economic conditions can influence an area's rate (Pew). Age and circumstance: in the 2022 BJS survey, younger people and people with lower incomes were far more likely than older, higher-income people to report violent victimization (Pew). Circumstance also shapes reporting: in 2022, roughly 8 in 10 motor vehicle thefts were reported to police, but only about 2 in 10 rapes or sexual assaults were (Pew, citing BJS): the same system, very different reporting behavior. Patterns exist; reading them well starts with asking who is counted and how.

collegeVersion.heading: Two honest notes
collegeVersion.body: First, the reality check on fear: public worry can outrun the numbers. FBI and BJS statistics both show U.S. violent and property crime rates fell sharply from the early 1990s to the early 2020s — the FBI's violent crime rate dropped 49% between 1993 and 2022, and BJS measured steeper declines (Pew). Yet in 23 of 27 Gallup surveys since 1993, at least 6 in 10 U.S. adults said there was more crime nationally than the year before (Pew). The fear is real; the trend it describes is not always. Second, the reality check on meaning: crime is a social mirror. What becomes law, what gets reported, who gets counted, and what gets feared all reflect a society's choices and circumstances, not a neutral tally of wrongdoing. Reading crime statistics is partly reading the society that produced them.

vocabulary.definition: Behavior that violates official law and is punishable through formal sanctions; the working definition used in OpenStax's Introduction to Sociology.
Behavior that departs from a group's social norms; deviance is a norm violation, while crime is a law violation, and the two are not the same.
The body of laws a society adopts and enforces through a political authority; breaking a legal code carries formal consequences.
A crime based on the use of force or the threat of force, such as murder, rape, or armed robbery.
A nonviolent crime involving the destruction or theft of property without the use of force, such as larceny, car theft, or vandalism.
A crime committed by someone working in a business or professional environment, such as embezzlement, insider trading, or identity theft.
A debated category of illegal acts in which the person committing them is not explicitly harming anyone else, such as underage drinking.
The FBI's annual compilation of crimes reported to law enforcement agencies across the United States; it misses crimes that are never reported.
The Bureau of Justice Statistics' annual survey of a national sample of U.S. residents age 12 and older about crimes they experienced, including crimes never reported to police.
A penalty imposed through official channels for breaking a written rule, such as a fine or imprisonment.

eli10.simplifiedExplanation: Crime is behavior that breaks the written law of a place and can be punished through formal channels — fines, courts, prison. It is not the same as deviance, which is breaking unwritten social rules: staring at your phone during a wedding is deviant but legal, while parking in a fire lane is a crime even if nobody is around. Sociologists sort crimes into broad types — violent, property, white-collar, and debated victimless ones — and count them two ways: police reports and large surveys. Each way misses something, because not every crime is reported and not every survey reaches everyone. Rates vary by place, age, and circumstance, and people's fear of crime often runs ahead of the data.
eli10.analogy: Think of crime statistics as a map drawn from streetlights rather than from the streets. The FBI's UCR lights only the spots where someone called it in — reported crimes; the NCVS is a flashlight that sweeps the same streets asking people directly what happened to them, catching crimes the streetlights missed. One map shows the lit-up crimes; the other shows more of the dark ones. Together they give a better picture than either alone — but both still miss the unlit corners where nobody reports and nobody is asked.
eli10.analogyLimits: A map shows whatever streets it covers; crime statistics show only what societies record, report, and ask about. Fear, stigma, distrust, and uneven participation by police agencies all dim the picture, so the reflection is never the whole scene — and unlike a map, the numbers themselves shape what people see and fear next.

workedExample: Priya, a journalism student, is assigned to write about safety in her city. She pulls the FBI's UCR table: burglaries fell 12% from the year before. Then she reads the BJS notes behind the NCVS and sees that in 2022, only 41.5% of violent crimes and 31.8% of household property crimes nationally were reported to police. She interviews neighbors anyway, and several describe incidents they never reported — a stolen bike, a threatening message — because they doubted anything would come of it. Priya's article leads with the official number, then adds the honest line: the statistics are the reported floor, not the full picture.

commonMistakes.mistake: "Crime and deviance are the same thing."
commonMistakes.correction: Deviance is a violation of social norms; crime is a violation of formal law. The two overlap, but an act can be one without the other — walking backward to class is deviant yet legal, while driving over the legal alcohol limit is a crime.

commonMistakes.mistake: "The UCR counts all crime in the United States."
commonMistakes.correction: The UCR compiles only crimes reported to police. Many crimes go unreported — out of fear, shame, distrust of police, or the belief that nothing would be done — and not every agency participates every year.

commonMistakes.mistake: "Crime rates have been climbing for decades."
commonMistakes.correction: FBI and BJS data both show U.S. violent and property crime rates fell sharply from the early 1990s to the early 2020s. Year-to-year bumps occur within that long-term decline, but the long-run trend is down.

commonMistakes.mistake: "Victimless crime is an official legal category."
commonMistakes.correction: It is a debated sociological label for illegal acts in which no one other than the actor is explicitly harmed. Critics argue such acts do harm society, so sociologists treat the label as contested, not fixed.
The NCVS interviews living victims, so it cannot count homicide. That is exactly why researchers pair the survey with police-based data such as the UCR.

compareContrast.distinction: Crime violates official law and draws formal sanctions such as fines or imprisonment; deviance violates social norms and draws informal reactions such as stares or disapproval. The circles overlap, but some acts fall in only one: walking backward to class is deviant but not criminal; driving over the legal alcohol limit is criminal.

The UCR compiles crimes reported to police from thousands of law enforcement agencies; the NCVS is a national household survey that asks people about victimizations, including crimes never reported. The UCR misses unreported crime; the NCVS cannot count murder and misses people without stable addresses.

Violent crime is based on the use of force or the threat of force against a person; property crime involves the destruction or theft of property without force. Prying open a car with a crowbar is a property crime; mugging someone with that crowbar is a violent crime.

keyTakeaway: Crime is behavior that violates official law — a distinct concept from deviance, a set of debated types, and a quantity no single measure fully captures. Crime data come from police reports and surveys, and reading them honestly means remembering both what they count and what they miss — and that fear can outrun the data.

questionBank.prompt: A student needs a one-sentence working definition of crime for a sociology paper. Which option captures the definition used in OpenStax's Introduction to Sociology?
options: Behavior that violates official law and is punishable through formal sanctions
Any behavior that a community disapproves of, whether written down or not
Behavior that violates social norms and draws informal disapproval
Any act that causes harm to another person, whether or not a law covers it
questionBank.explanation: OpenStax's section 7.3 defines crime as behavior that violates official law and is punishable through formal sanctions. Option B describes disapproval without law; C is the definition of deviance, which is a norm violation; and D describes harm, which is not part of the working definition and is not always criminalized.
questionBank.skill: Recalling the working definition of crime and its source

questionBank.prompt: Ravi, a sociology student, walks backward across campus to his morning lecture; people stare, but no rule forbids it. That same evening his roommate drives home after three drinks, above the state's legal blood-alcohol limit, and is stopped by police. How would sociologists classify the two acts?
options: Both acts are crimes, because both draw negative reactions
Both acts are deviant, because both violate social norms
Walking backward is deviance (a norm violation); driving over the legal limit is a crime (a law violation)
Walking backward is a crime; driving over the limit is deviance
questionBank.explanation: OpenStax's section 7.3 distinguishes deviance, a violation of social norms, from crime, a violation of official law — walking backward to class is its own example of deviance that is not a crime, while driving over the legal alcohol limit is a crime. Option A confuses reactions with law; B fits the first act but not the second, which breaks written law regardless of norms; D reverses both labels.
questionBank.skill: Applying the crime-versus-deviance distinction to original scenarios

questionBank.prompt: Over two years, a payroll clerk at a small credit union quietly reroutes fractions of employee paychecks into a personal account, draining the credit union's reserves and costing members their savings. How would sociologists classify this offense?
options: A violent crime, because it harmed many victims
A street crime, because it involved theft
A victimless crime, because no physical injury occurred
A white-collar (corporate) crime, committed within a business environment
questionBank.explanation: OpenStax's section 7.3 defines corporate, or white-collar, crime as crime committed by white-collar workers in a business environment — embezzlement is a named example. Option A is wrong because no force or threat of force was used; B misses the setting, which is what makes it white-collar rather than street crime; C is wrong because embezzlement has clear victims — the employees and members who lost money.
questionBank.skill: Classifying a described offense by sociological crime type

questionBank.prompt: Which statement correctly describes the two main U.S. national sources of crime data?
options: The UCR is a household survey, and the NCVS is a compilation of police reports
The UCR compiles crimes reported to police; the NCVS surveys people about victimizations, including crimes never reported
Both the UCR and the NCVS count only crimes that end in a conviction
Both the UCR and the NCVS interview the same 240,000 people every year
questionBank.explanation: The FBI's Uniform Crime Reports compile crimes reported to law enforcement, while the BJS National Crime Victimization Survey interviews a national sample of about 240,000 people and captures crimes both reported and not reported to police (BJS; Pew Research Center). Option A swaps the two programs; C confuses reporting with conviction, which neither measure requires; D is wrong because the UCR is not a survey at all.
questionBank.skill: Recalling what the UCR and the NCVS each measure

questionBank.prompt: Polling summarized by Pew Research Center found that in 23 of 27 Gallup surveys since 1993, at least 6 in 10 U.S. adults said crime nationally was higher than the year before — even while FBI and BJS data showed violent and property crime rates falling sharply over most of that period. What does this pattern best illustrate?
options: Public fear of crime can outrun the official data
Police reports capture the true level of unreported crime
Survey measures of victimization are less reliable than police reports
U.S. crime rates rose steadily through the 1990s and 2000s
questionBank.explanation: Pew Research Center reports that Americans tend to believe crime is up even when official data shows it is down, with the Gallup pattern as evidence. Option B contradicts the sources: police reports miss unreported crime, which is why the NCVS exists; C reverses the usual reading, since the NCVS captures crimes police never see; D contradicts FBI and BJS data showing long-term declines from the early 1990s.
questionBank.skill: Analyzing the gap between public perception and official crime statistics

provenance.rightsStatus: reference-only sources (OpenStax Introduction to Sociology 3e, CC BY 4.0; Bureau of Justice Statistics NCVS overview, U.S. government work; Pew Research Center short read, copyright Pew); facts synthesized in original wording, no source prose adapted; all examples original
provenance.transformation: Working definition of crime (behavior that violates official law, punishable through formal sanctions), the crime-versus-deviance distinction, legal codes, the violent/property/white-collar/victimless crime typology, the UCR police-report basis and its unreported-crime gap, the NCVS survey design and its limits (no murder, misses mobile populations), and the point that the UCR and NCVS together still do not capture all crime, all verified against OpenStax Introduction to Sociology 3e section 7.3 (read via Wayback Machine capture of the canonical URL, 2026-04-22). Current NCVS design (nationally representative sample of about 240,000 persons in about 150,000 households, age 12 and older, capturing crimes both reported and not reported to police) verified against the Bureau of Justice Statistics NCVS overview page (read live 2026-08-22). Long-term U.S. crime-rate declines since the early 1990s (FBI violent -49%, property -59%, 1993-2022; BJS declines), the 2022 reporting rates (41.5% of violent and 31.8% of household property crimes reported), patterns by age, income, and state (2022 FBI and BJS data), and the Gallup perception pattern (23 of 27 surveys since 1993 with at least 6 in 10 adults saying national crime rose) verified against Pew Research Center's 'What the data says about crime in the U.S.' (read live 2026-08-22). All examples (dawn stop-sign cyclist, sandals-at-interview student, knife convenience-store holdup, tire slashing, payroll-clerk embezzlement, 18-year-old's beer, Priya's reporting exercise) are original to this lesson.
